newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan prices rising but no inflation seen.
newsitem.headline: Japan prices rising but no inflation seen.

text.p: Japanese prices are expected to provide little inflationary pressure over the next business year, economists said in a Reuters poll released on Thursday.
"If the Bank of Japan decides to change monetary policy over the next business year, it's not going to be because of prices," said Yasuhiko Ushikubo, an economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan.
The forecasts from 35 economists produced a mean average rise of 1.4 percent in consumer prices for fiscal 1997/98, with forecasts ranging from 0.8 percent to 1.9 percent
The economists said that while this meant a substantial rise from the average 0.3 percent forecast for the current business year, it was mostly attributable to an expected sales tax hike.
"If you take out the the consumption tax hike, prices are flat or will rise something like 0.2 percent year on year -- virtually nothing," said Ushikubo.
The government plans to raise the sales tax to five percent from three percent in April, the beginning of the fiscal year.

Wholesale prices were also expected to show a mild increase, with the forecasts of 32 economists showing an average rise of 1.1 percent compared with a 0.7 percent increase forecast for fiscal 1996/97.
They said a weakening in the yen would boost import prices for raw materials, but tough competition between companies would mean firms had to absorb the costs themselves.
The latest available data at the time of the survey showed national consumer prices up 0.5 percent year on year and wholesale prices down 0.6 percent year on year for November.
The survey covered 37 brokerages and research bodies, although not all those polled responded to all the questions.
The survey was conducted between January 13 and 16.
